I see! At line 4074: `hoedown_buffer_grow(text, size)` - this grows the `text` buffer to `size` bytes (the input size). But `size` is `ib->size`, which is the size of the input data.

For my PoC with 64 bytes: `hoedown_buffer_grow(text, 64)` → `text->asize = 64`. Then data is copied into `text` via `expand_tabs`. The `text->size` becomes the size of the copied data.

But wait, at line 4151-4152:
```c
if (text->data[text->size - 1] != '\n')
    hoedown_buffer_putc(text, '\n');
```

This adds a newline if the last character is not a newline. `hoedown_buffer_putc` calls `hoedown_buffer_grow(text, text->size + 1)` which grows the buffer to `text->asize + text->unit = 64 + 64 = 128` bytes. So `text->asize` becomes 128!

This means the buffer is now 128 bytes, and the OOB read at `text->data[64]` is within the buffer!

Hmm, but the newline is only added if `text->data[text->size - 1] != '\n'`. In my PoC, the last character is a space (not a newline), so a newline is added, growing the buffer to 128 bytes.

Let me check: in my PoC, the last 4 bytes are `\n   ` (newline + 3 spaces). So `text->data[text->size - 1]` is a space, not a newline. So a newline is added, growing the buffer.

But wait, the newline is added AFTER the data is copied. So `text->size` becomes 65 (64 bytes of data + 1 newline). And `text->asize` becomes 128 (grown from 64 to 128).

Then `parse_block(ob, doc, text->data, text->size)` is called with `text->size = 65`. Inside `parse_block`, `parse_fencedcode` is called with `txt_data = text->data` and `end = 65`.

In `parse_fencedcode`, the loop processes lines:
- Line 0: ```` ``` ```` (opening fence) → `i = 4` (after the newline)
- Lines 1-28: `a\n` → `i` advances
- Line 29: `\n` (empty line before the 3 spaces) → `i` advances
- Line 30: `   ` (3 spaces) → `line_start = 61`, `i = 64` (no newline)
- `is_codefence(data + 61, 3, ...)` → `data[3] = text->data[64]`

But `text->data[64]` is the newline that was added at line 4152! So `text->data[64]` is within the buffer (which is now 128 bytes).

So the OOB read is at `text->data[64]`, which is within the allocated buffer. ASAN won't catch this.

I need to make the OOB read go past the allocated buffer. Let me think about how to do this...

The `text` buffer is grown to `size` bytes (the input size). Then data is copied into it. Then a newline is added if needed, growing the buffer further.

If the input size is exactly 64 bytes, and the last character is a newline, then no newline is added, and `text->asize = 64`. But then the last line would be `   \n` (3 spaces + newline), and `is_codefence` would be called with `size = 3` (excluding the newline). `data[3]` would read the newline, which is at `text->data[63]` (the last byte of the buffer). This is within the buffer.

If the input size is exactly 64 bytes, and the last character is a space (no newline), then a newline is added, growing the buffer to 128 bytes. `text->asize = 128`. The OOB read at `text->data[64]` is within the buffer.

I need a different approach. Let me think about what happens if the input size is not a multiple of 64...

If the input size is 65 bytes, then `hoedown_buffer_grow(text, 65)` → `text->asize = 128` (grown from 0 to 128 in one step: `neoasz = 0 + 64 = 64`, `while (64 < 65)` → `neoasz = 128`, `while (128 < 65)` → false). So `text->asize = 128`.

Then data is copied into `text`. `text->size = 65`. If the last character is a newline, no newline is added. `parse_block` is called with `text->size = 65`.

If the last line is `   ` (3 spaces) at position 62-64, then `is_codefence(data + 62, 3, ...)` → `data[3] = text->data[65]`. But `text->asize = 128`, so `text->data[65]` is within the buffer.

Hmm, this is tricky. The buffer is always oversized because of the unit-based allocation.

Wait, let me re-examine the problem. Maybe the vulnerability is not about reading past the allocated buffer, but about reading past the specified `size` parameter. The `is_codefence` function is called with `size = 3` (the line length), but it reads `data[3]` which is past the specified size. This is an OOB read relative to the line, not relative to the buffer.
